introduction: The study aimed to explore psychiatric inpatients’ experiences of exercise and its perceived impact on mental well-being during hospitalization. The authors note that research on exercise among psychiatric inpatients remains limited, and that less is known about how these patients experience exercise.
methodology: A qualitative study with a purposive sample of eight inpatients (five male, three female; mean age 53.9) at the University Hospital of North Norway, who had taken part in individualized exercise sessions with an exercise physiologist. Participants were recruited by an exercise physiologist and took part in a telephone interview, using a semi-structured guide with open-ended questions. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis.
theory: The analysis took a contextualist perspective.
results: Four themes were identified: follow-up support, symptom reduction, sense of mastery, and activation during hospitalization. Support from the exercise physiologists was highlighted as a crucial factor for initiating and maintaining exercise. Many described how exercise instantly helped reduce anxiety, anger, and depressive symptoms. The perceived effects were not uniformly strong, and some participants were uncertain about effects on sleep or energy.
discussion: The authors suggest that adequate support and follow-up are key to implementing physical exercise interventions for inpatients in psychiatric care, and that more inpatients should be given the opportunity to participate in regular physical exercise. They state that the findings reflect participants’ subjective experiences and should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment efficacy or causal effects of exercise. They describe physical activity as a supplement to established interventions rather than a replacement for them.
limitations: The authors note that the sample of eight participants is relatively small, and that a possible selection bias may exist because those who chose to participate may have been more positively inclined toward exercise. They state that the single-center Norwegian setting may limit transferability, that the study had no comparator, and that telephone interviews limited access to non-verbal cues. They call for future research with a broader and more diverse sample, including psychiatric inpatients specifically, and for further research to examine efficacy and identify active components of the exercise intervention.

methodology.q: This was a qualitative study, based on a purposive sample of eight inpatients who had participated in individualized physical exercise sessions supported by exercise physiologists.
The study took place in the Division of Substance Use and Mental Health at the University Hospital of North Norway.
the single-center Norwegian setting may limit the transferability of the findings to other inpatient settings
The participants had a mean age of 53.9 (range from 31 to 84). Five were male and three were female.
The participants were recruited by an exercise physiologist (S.R.), who asked inpatients if they wanted to participate in a qualitative study.
The participants suffered from schizoaffective disorder/schizophrenia
The interview guide was semi-structured, with open-ended questions.
Each participant took part in a telephone interview lasting approximately 30 minutes (range 20–60 minutes).
All interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim.
the transcriptions were analysed by drawing on principles from reflexive thematic analysis

theory.q: The analysis was carried out with a contextualist perspective.

results.q: The participants’ responses were divided into four main themes: 1) ‘Follow-up support’, 2) ‘Symptom reduction’, 3) ‘Sense of mastery’ and 4) ‘Activation during hospitalization’.
Support from the exercise physiologists was highlighted as a crucial factor for initiating and maintaining exercise.

The participants stated that they experienced that exercising led to improvements in mood and emotional balance. Many described how exercise instantly helped reduce anxiety, anger, and depressive symptoms.

However, the perceived effects were not uniformly strong. Some participants were uncertain whether exercise affected specific symptoms such as sleep or energy, and one participant reported little noticeable change in some areas.

discussion.q: These findings reflect participants’ subjective experiences and should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment efficacy or causal effects of exercise.
Our results suggest that adequate support and follow-up are key to successfully implementing physical exercise interventions for inpatients in psychiatric care.
The results may suggest that more inpatients should be given the opportunity to participate in regular physical exercise.
Physical activity should therefore be viewed as a supplement to established interventions for the treatment of mental illness.
Exercise can serve as a treatment in addition to medication and psychotherapy during hospitalization, but it is typically not intended to replace standard treatment.

limitations.q: the sample size of eight participants is relatively small
A second limitation is a possible selection bias, as those who chose to participate may have been more positively inclined toward exercise.
This may have introduced selection and social desirability bias
Caution is required when considering the transferability of our findings to other settings or populations.

As exercise was provided within ongoing inpatient treatment and the study had no comparator, it is difficult to distinguish the perceived effects of exercise from those of other aspects of inpatient treatment.
telephone-based interviews limited access to non-verbal cues
Future studies should aim to include a broader and more diverse sample to capture a wider range of experiences.
Future research on the importance of physical exercise in psychiatric treatment should place greater emphasis on psychiatric inpatients

Further research is needed to examine efficacy, identify active components of the exercise intervention, and understand how exercise can be effectively integrated into inpatient treatment and sustained beyond discharge.

abstract_claims.q: We identified four key themes: follow-up support, symptom reduction, sense of mastery, and activation during hospitalization.
A particularly notable finding was that participants reported immediate improvements in mood and perceived mental well-being following exercise.
The presence of an exercise physiologist was described as a crucial source of motivation and support.
Overall, the study suggests that structured opportunities for exercise with individualized professional support may be a valuable component of psychiatric inpatient care.

caveats.q: Given the small and heterogeneous sample, subgroup analyses were not performed.
